pending_items.title: Israel's Eisenkot agrees to coalition deal with left-wing Democrats
pending_items.content:
The centrist party of former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot , who is trying to form the next Israeli government , and an allied left-wing party on Thursday announced they had agreed on a coalition deal.

The left-leaning Democrats are the second party to agree to a coalition deal with Eisenkot's Yashar after the right-wing Israel Beiteinu party, headed by Avigdor Lieberman , did so on Tuesday, marking a further step towards forming a government.

Eisenkot has until December 6 – a deadline which can be extended by 14 days – to form a government to replace caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after the October election failed to deliver a clear majority for either bloc.

"Gadi Eisenkot, chair of Yashar with Eisenkot, and Yair Golan, chair of the Democrats, have agreed to sign a coalition agreement between the two parties," a joint statement said on Thursday.

The Democrats said they would receive four ministerial portfolios as part of the coalition deal, including an expanded national security ministry which under Netanyahu's government is headed by the far-right Itamar Ben-Gvir .

Watch more Writer Etgar Keret: 'The Israel my parents dreamed of' is still possible, but not under Netanyahu

The party will also receive the Ministry of Labour, Ministry of Communications, and Ministry of Culture and Sport, which will include a new directorate for democracy, the party said in a statement.

"We promised the people that we ​would replace Netanyahu and defend democracy. And that is what we will do," Golan said in ‌a post on X .

"I call on all parties to come together as soon as possible to finalise agreements and sign them, form a government, and lead Israel in a new direction. This is the mission of our lives."

Eisenkot, Lieberman and Golan have a combined total of 36 lawmakers – far short of the 61 needed for a parliamentary majority.

The bloc also includes the Beyachad party of former prime minister Naftali Bennett , which has 12 seats but is yet to sign a formal coalition agreement with Yashar.

Eisenkot's wide-ranging anti-Netanyahu camp has faced divisions on whether to forge alliances with the ultra-Orthodox parties, or the Arab-majority lists, or whether to form a national unity government with Netanyahu's right-wing Likud .

The Democrats have been pushing Eisenkot for an alliance with two Arab-majority lists that achieved an unprecedented seat haul in the vote, in a bid to unseat Netanyahu.

The party disapproved of the four rounds of talks between Yashar and Likud in recent days exploring the possibility of a unity government. No breakthroughs on that front have ostensibly been reached.

Lieberman, on the other hand, has refused to serve in a government that relies on Arab-majority parties and has instead advocated an alliance with the two ultra-Orthodox parties, despite his years of criticism of the community and the fact that the issue of ultra-Orthodox military conscription remains a thorny one.

On Thursday, Lieberman warned that Netanyahu was trying to derail the government's formation.

"He will drag out negotiations over a 'unity' government until the last moment, look for a pretext to blow them up, and even if such a government is formed, he will try to engineer a crisis within a few months to drag Israel back to elections," added Lieberman, a hawkish former aide to Netanyahu who has become a strident critic.

Bennett, meanwhile, has been pushing for a unity government between Eisenkot's bloc and Likud that would exclude the ultra-Orthodox and Arab parties.

"Even at this time, I believe that by far the best alternative for the State of Israel and the serving public is a Zionist unity government led by Eisenkot first," he wrote on X, referring to a possible rotation agreement for the premiership.

pending_items.title: Exclusive-US pushed Venezuela, Iraq to consider leaving OPEC, sources say
pending_items.content:
By Ahmad Ghaddar, Ahmed Rasheed and Marianna Parraga

LONDON/BAGHDAD/HOUSTON, Nov 27 (Reuters) - The Trump administration encouraged Venezuela and Iraq to consider leaving OPEC earlier this year and prevented Venezuela from paying its annual membership dues to the group, according to ten people familiar with the matter.

The previously unreported moves targeted two of OPEC's five founding members, marking an unusually direct challenge to an organization President Donald Trump has long accused of keeping oil prices artificially high.

US officials were pushing for greater oil production and investment in both countries at the time, and some worried OPEC production limits could eventually constrain those ambitions, according to people familiar with the discussions.

The US pressure on Venezuela went far enough that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman intervened this summer, persuading the Trump administration not to press the issue further, two people familiar with the matter said.

In Iraq, Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi raised the possibility of leaving OPEC at a government meeting this summer after discussions with US officials who encouraged the idea, two people familiar with the matter said.

Iraq's oil ministry pushed back, persuading al-Zaidi to keep Iraq in the group and consider seeking a higher production quota instead, the people said.

The United States has powerful leverage over both countries. The US controls Venezuela's access to state funds following the January ouster of Nicolas Maduro, while Iraq's oil revenues continue to pass through an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, a relic of the 2003 Iraq War.

The US State Department did not answer questions about whether it had prevented Venezuela from paying its OPEC membership fee. But it confirmed Washington has the power to decide on Venezuela’s use of state funds, now held in a US-controlled account set up after Maduro's removal.

"The Department receives disbursement requests from the interim Venezuelan government and reviews the requests, including against a list of approved and prohibited uses of the foreign Government Deposit Funds," a State Department official told Reuters.

The official said that it was possible that lower-level US officials had raised the question of leaving OPEC with Venezuela's government earlier this year, but that "it has not been among the issues raised by high-level officials."

The State Department's conversations with Iraq, meanwhile, "have focused on improving energy infrastructure to increase production and transportation of energy, not OPEC," the official said.

Representatives for OPEC and for the governments of Venezuela, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia did not respond to requests for comment.

The US maneuvers add strain to an organization that has already lost four members since 2019, and whose share of the global oil market recently hit a low on the back of disruptions caused by the US and Israeli war on Iran, another OPEC founding member.

"The risk of OPEC fracture is rising," said Dan Alamariu, chief geopolitical strategist at Alpine Macro.

The United Arab Emirates announced its exit from OPEC earlier this year after becoming frustrated with the group’s production caps, while Angola, Ecuador and Qatar quit the group in 2024, 2020 and 2019, respectively. There are no indications the US was involved in those decisions.

OPEC was founded in Baghdad in September 1960 by oil producer countries seeking to assert more control over a global market that had become dominated by a small handful of Western oil companies.

Founded by Iraq, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Venezuela, OPEC is now made up of 11 members. It has also developed an alliance with several other producer countries including Russia called OPEC+, which regularly meets to decide on coordinated production levels.

Trump has repeatedly attacked OPEC throughout his decades-long business and political career, calling it a cartel and a monopoly profiting from the rest of the world. Over the past decade, though, the US has become the world's largest oil producer, turning it from an OPEC customer into its main rival for oil market share.

After the US seized Maduro in January, the US State Department opened discussions with Venezuelan officials in Washington on whether the country should leave OPEC, five people familiar with the matter told Reuters.

They did not identify the individuals who took part in those discussions.

Trump wanted US oil majors to revive Venezuela's oil output - something he said would shore up energy security in the Western Hemisphere - and worried that OPEC policy decisions could hinder that plan, the sources said.

Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman intervened, however, persuading the Trump administration not to push further, two of the sources said. Saudi Arabia is OPEC’s top producer and its de facto leader.

In August, Trump said it was up to Venezuela whether to leave OPEC.

US officials this summer also held talks with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi, encouraging Iraq's departure from OPEC as US oil majors Exxon Mobil and Chevron planned major new investments there, two people familiar with the matter said.

Al-Zaidi later raised the issue at a government meeting. His oil ministry persuaded him to stay and instead potentially seek a higher OPEC quota, they said.

The issue could come up again since some elements of Iraq’s ruling coalition are favorable to leaving OPEC and OPEC+, which they view as dominated by Saudi Arabia and Russia, the people said.

There is no indication Washington has sought to block Baghdad’s OPEC dues.

After the US invasion of Iraq in 2003, the United States began routing Iraq's oil revenues through an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. That structure remains in place more than two decades later.

This year, the US threatened to starve Iraq of its oil money if it didn’t cut Iran’s influence in its government.

OPEC membership fee payments are typically due in the first quarter of each year, and pay for staff salaries, research, and travel at the OPEC Secretariat in Vienna.

Unlike the United Nations, where dues are scaled to the size of a country's economy, OPEC splits the fees equally among members at around 2.8 million euros ($3.08 million) each.

The price tag is tiny compared to OPEC oil revenues, but paying it carries symbolic importance as a marker of continued membership in an organization Caracas helped create.

Washington argued money from Venezuela could be spent on more important matters, one of the people familiar with the country's relationship with OPEC said.

OPEC has the discretion to disregard unpaid membership fees, and is not planning to expel Venezuela over the issue, two OPEC sources told Reuters.

Washington's control of Venezuela's oil revenues and finances has led some in the South American country to refer to their country as a US protectorate, instead of a sovereign nation.

The US Government Accountability Office opened a formal investigation in July into the administration’s management and disbursement of Venezuelan oil revenues, following congressional requests for transparency.

The Trump administration has said Venezuela's oil revenues are being used to meet the needs of the Venezuelan people, including to pay government salaries and fund essential services.

Reuters could not establish when exactly the US rejected the OPEC dues payment request.

Venezuela is currently exempt from OPEC+ oil output quotas as its production has collapsed from historical highs due to years of sanctions and mismanagement.

The country pumped about 1.2 million barrels per day in September, according to OPEC figures. Its state oil company PDVSA has said it plans to reach 1.5 million bpd by the end of next year.

OPEC last regulated Caracas' output with quotas in 2017-2018 when the country’s target was around 2 million bpd. The country's return to the quota system is unlikely until it hits that level again, a source familiar with Venezuela's OPEC position said.

(Additional reporting by Jonathan Saul and Timothy Gardner; Writing by Alex Lawler and Dmitry Zhdannikov; Editing by Veronica Brown and Richard Valdmanis)

pending_items.title: ‘You can’t stop it’: Indians embrace Pakistani dramas, defying bans
pending_items.content:
When New Delhi-based cultural impresario and curator Abu Sufiyan Khan organised a recent screening of the Pakistani romantic drama Dar-e-Nijaat in the Indian capital, he was stunned. It was meant to be a private event for 45 people, at most. Khan got more than 700 requests for attendance.

Like all other Pakistani shows and songs, Dar-e-Nijaat is officially banned in India. Yet every weekend, Indian viewers gather on Instagram to exchange clips, debate episodes and celebrate its leading character, Abu Bakr.

Offline, watch parties and group screenings are organised in different parts of the country. As the craze for the show – which involves a young woman Zaryab, her childhood love Zamil, and Abu Bakr, who later steps into Zaryab’s life to fill a void – has gripped Indian cities, the police have been left playing cat-and-mouse.

At least two screenings in the southern city of Bengaluru, scheduled for this coming weekend, have now been cancelled after authorities saw posters advertising the events. But those attempts at a crackdown haven’t dimmed the appeal of the show.

One phrase, repeated across fan pages and comment sections, has become a shorthand for its craze: “Sabr ka phal nahi, Abu Bakr chahiye,” (We don’t want the reward of patience; we want Abu Bakr.)

It is a playful twist on a familiar Urdu proverb, and an indication of the affection Indian viewers have developed for a fictional Pakistani man. “We have all been looking forward to an Abu Bakr. I have been going gaga over him because of how empathetic he is, and that is what is missing in most of the men these days,” says Rakhshanda Mujib, a fan from Bengaluru.

Yet the excitement over Dar-e-Nijaat is only the latest expression of a much wider appetite. India’s efforts to keep Pakistani entertainment off its screens have done little to extinguish the appetite for it.

“Indians cannot approach Pakistani artists on Instagram, access Pakistani music on Spotify or view Pakistani dramas without VPNs or proxies on YouTube,” Sufiyan Khan said.

But for many, the forbidden fruit of Pakistani culture remains alluring enough to risk breaching the official ban.

Despite multiple wars and near-perpetual tensions, India and Pakistan had for decades allowed cultural exchanges – even though they each periodically imposed restrictions.

But informal bans on Pakistani artistes working or performing in India gained ground over the past decade as Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government in New Delhi increasingly dialled down all contact with Pakistan to a bare minimum.

A new tipping point arrived in April 2025, when gunmen killed 26 tourists in Pahalgam, in Indian-administered Kashmir. India blamed Pakistan for the attack, while Islamabad denied any role. The neighbours fought an intense four-day war before agreeing to a ceasefire.

Since then, India has banned all Pakistani songs, movies and dramas from streaming platforms, including YouTube. It has cited national security for its decision. This week, it demanded that Netflix take down – from viewing in India – Pakistan’s first show on that platform.

Yet while China imposed a similar ban on Korean pop culture in 2016, and it held for the better part of a decade, India’s efforts appear to be failing.

The reason lies in where the chokepoint sits. China controls the platforms its citizens use. India does not control YouTube. Section 69A of India’s Information Technology Act lets the government direct platforms to block content, and the orders are generally confidential. In practice, YouTube geo-blocked Pakistani channels for users in India.

But a geo-block governs a platform, not a viewer. A VPN changes where a viewer appears to be, and anyone who downloads a drama that way can re-upload it from an account inside India.

On May 8, 2025 – the day streaming platforms were told to drop Pakistani content – searches for VPNs in India rose 72 percent, according to the monitoring firm Top10VPN, which links the rise to both governments blocking each other’s online content.

Those VPNs downloaded in India translate into good business for Pakistani channels like ARY Digital, the network behind Dar-e-Nijaat.

“Indian viewers account for 30 to 35 percent of total views for Pakistani channels”, says Jerjees Seja, head of ARY Entertainment. “In this day and age, you can make access to content difficult, but you can’t stop it.”

Seja’s assertion is hard to dispute. The 2022 drama Tere Bin and the 2024 soap Kabhi Main Kabhi Tum were both also wildly popular in India. Pakistani director Mehreen Jabbar says viewers in India message her about her series such as Dr Bahu, Jackson Heights and Daam.

So, what makes these shows click for Indian audiences?

Culturally, the similarities between India and Pakistan mean that a lot that’s seen in Pakistani shows is instantly relatable for many across the border. Seja adds that Pakistan’s entertainment industry has also grown in its quality of production. “Our content has become very strong over the years,” he said. “It is realistic, on-the-ground, thought-provoking, and relatable.”

But there’s another reason, too, suggests Sufiyan Khan, that dramas like Dar-e-Nijaat find a willing audience in India. Far too often, Indian shows and movies stereotype Muslim characters. By contrast, Dar-e-Nijaat’s appeal, he said, lies in part in its “exceptional portrayal of Islam as not being threatening or Bollywood-style performative with kohl eyes and prayer caps but a refreshing, non-judgmental and inclusive Islam where all the rituals are being practised with humility”.

Culture is inconvenient in wartime politics because it makes an enemy familiar. But technology has made it harder for governments to firewall entire societies.

“Over the last few years, a whole wave of Indian people are consuming Pakistani TV shows, music and influencer content. There has been a democratisation of culture and access, which has led to the breaking of stereotypes,” said Aishwarya Verma, a policy analyst in Delhi. “Back in the day, we didn’t know too much about our brothers and sisters across the border, and vice versa.”

Pakistani actress and singer Haniya Aamer, for instance, is popular for her music in India. A recent song by her, Pablo, features Indian actress Rakhi Sawant. “We’re all listening to her music,” said Verma. “Who would have thought?”

Ajay Bisaria, former Indian high commissioner to Pakistan, said bans of the kind India has imposed rarely work. “Technology changes. It makes both borders and bans less relevant. Governments impose bans because culture is visible and easy to restrict. Pakistan has done the same: Indian films were banned there for decades.”

Yet, as with Pakistani shows in India, Bollywood thrived on pirated cassettes in Pakistan.

“Culture”, Bisaria said, “has played a massive binding force in the bilateral relationship between India and Pakistan, whether the two nations have wanted it or not.” And Dar-e-Nijaat shows it continues to do so.
